entries.a75f45b16e7e6ae318e48f4bdc272afd501def25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv117"/><title type="x-ms">Philippians</title> <div sID="gen31907" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31908" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Philippi</hi> was a chief city of the western part of Macedonia, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prote tes meridos tes Makedonias polis,</hi></hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">Acts xvi. 12</reference>. It took its name from Philip, the famous king of Macedon, who repaired and beautified it, and it was afterwards made a Roman colony. Near this place were the <hi type="italic">Campi Philippici,</hi> remarkable for the famous battles between Julius Cæsar and Pompey the Great, and that between Augustus and Antony on one side and Cassius and Brutus on the other. But it is most remarkable among Christians for this epistle, which was written when Paul was a prisoner at Rome, A.D. 62. Paul seems to have had a very particular kindness for the church at Philippi, which he himself had been instrumental in planting; and, though he had <hi type="italic">the care of all the churches,</hi> he had, upon that account, a particular fatherly tender care of this. To those to whom God has employed us to do any good we should look upon ourselves both as encouraged and engaged to study to do more good. He looked upon them as his children, and, having <hi type="italic">begotten them by the gospel,</hi> he was desirous by the same gospel to nourish and nurse them up. I. He was called in an extraordinary manner to preach the gospel at Philippi, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">Acts xvi. 9</reference>. A vision appeared to Paul in the night: <hi type="italic">There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.</hi> He saw God going before him, and was encouraged to use all means for carrying on the good work which was begun among them, and building upon the foundation which was laid. II. At Philippi he suffered hard things; he was scourged, and put into the stocks (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.23-Acts.16.24">Acts xvi. 23, 24</reference>); yet he had not the less kindness for the place for the hard usage he met with there. We must never love our friends the less for the ill treatment which our enemies give us. III. The beginnings of that church were very small; Lydia was converted there, and the jailer, and a few more: yet that did not discourage him. If good be not done at first, it may be done afterwards, and the last works may be more abundant. We must not be discouraged by small beginnings. IV. It seems, by many passages in this epistle, that this church at Philippi grew into a flourishing church, and particularly that the brethren were very kind to Paul. He had reaped of their temporal things, and he made a return in spiritual things. He acknowledges the receipt of a present they had sent him (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">iv. 18</reference>), and this when no other church communicated with him as concerning giving and receiving (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">v. 15</reference>); and he gives them a prophet's, an apostle's reward, in this epistle, which is of more value than thousands of gold and silver. <div eID="gen31908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31909" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31910" type="x-p"/> He begins with the inscription and benediction, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1-Phil.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. He gives thanks for the saints at Philippi, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.3-Phil.1.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. He speaks of his great affection and concern for their spiritual welfare (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.7-Phil.1.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), his prayers for them (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.9-Phil.1.11">ver. 9-11</reference>), his care to prevent their offence at his sufferings (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.12-Phil.1.20">ver. 12-20</reference>), his readiness to glorify Christ by life or death (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.21-Phil.1.26">ver. 21-26</reference>), and then concludes with a double exhortation to strictness and constancy, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.27-Phil.1.30">ver. 27-30</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv117"/> <div eID="gen31910" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31909" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostolic Benediction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31911" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: <hi type="super">2</hi> Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen31911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31912" type="x-p"/> We have here the inscription and benediction. Observe, <div eID="gen31912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31913" type="x-p"/> I. The persons writing the epistle—<hi type="italic">Paul and Timotheus.</hi> Though Paul was alone divinely inspired, he joins Timothy with himself, to express his own humility, and put honour upon Timothy. Those who are aged, and strong, and eminent, should pay respect to, and support the reputation of, those who are younger, and weaker, and of less note. <hi type="italic">The servants of Jesus Christ;</hi> not only in the common relation of his disciples, but in the peculiar work of the ministry, the high office of an apostle and an evangelist. Observe, The highest honour of the greatest apostle, and most eminent ministers, is to be the servants of Jesus Christ; not the masters of the churches, but the servants of Christ. Observe, <div eID="gen31913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31914" type="x-p"/> II. The persons to whom it is directed. 1. To <hi type="italic">all the saints in Christ who are at Philippi.</hi> He mentions the church before the ministers, because the ministers are for the church, for their edification and benefit, not the churches for the ministers, for their dignity, dominion, and wealth. <hi type="italic">Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.24">2 Cor. i. 24</reference>. They are not only the servants of Christ, but the servants of the church for his sake. <hi type="italic">Ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">2 Cor. iv. 5</reference>. Observe, The Christians here are called saints; set apart for God, or sanctified by his Spirit, either by visible profession or real holiness. And those who are not really saints on earth will never be saints in heaven. Observe, It is directed to <hi type="italic">all the saints,</hi> one as well as another, even the meanest, the poorest, and those of the least gifts. Christ makes no difference; the rich and the poor meet together in him: and the ministers must not make a difference in their care and tenderness upon these accounts. We must not <hi type="italic">have the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">James ii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Saints in Christ Jesus;</hi> saints are accepted only by virtue of their being in Christ Jesus, or as they are Christians. Out of Christ the best saints will appear sinners, and unable to stand before God. 2. It is directed to the ministers, or church-officers—<hi type="italic">with the bishops and deacons,</hi> the bishops or elders, in the first place, whose office it was to teach and rule, and the deacons, or overseers of the poor, who took care of the outward business of the house of God: the place, the furniture, the maintenance of the ministers, and provision for the poor. These were all the offices which were then known in the church, and which were of divine appointment. The apostle, in the direction of his epistle to a Christian church, acknowledges but two orders, which he calls bishops and deacons. And whosoever shall consider that the same characters and titles, the same qualifications, the same acts of office, and the same honour and respect, are every where ascribed throughout the New Testament to those who are called bishops and presbyters (as Dr. Hammond and other learned men allow), will find it difficult to make them a different office or distinct order of ministry in the scripture times. <div eID="gen31914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31915" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the apostolical benediction: <hi type="italic">Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.2">v. 2</reference>. This is the same, almost word for word, in all the epistles, to teach us that we must not be shy of forms, though we are not to be tied down to them, especially such as are not scriptural. The only form in the Old Testament is that of a benediction (<reference osisRef="Num.6.23-Num.6.26">Num. vi. 23-26</reference>), <hi type="italic">On this wise you shall bless the children of Israel, saying unto them, The Lord bless thee and keep thee: the Lord make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: the Lord lift up the light of his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.</hi> So in the New Testament, the good which is wished is spiritual good, <hi type="italic">grace and peace</hi>—the free favour and good-will of God, and all the blessed fruits and effects of it, and that <hi type="italic">from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> jointly from them both, though in a different way. Observe, 1. No peace without grace. Inward peace springs from a sense of divine favour. 2. No grace and peace but from God our Father, the fountain and original of all blessings, the <hi type="italic">Father of lights, from whom cometh down every good and perfect gift,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">James i. 17</reference>. 3. No grace and peace from God our Father, but in and through our Lord Jesus Christ. Christ, as Mediator, is the channel of conveyance of all spiritual blessings to the church, and directs the disposal of them to all his members.
entries.74808d9849624a537030bcf6d5711d9ffdaa246d: <div eID="gen31915" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Thankfulness and Joy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31916" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> I thank my God upon every remembrance of you, 4 Always in every prayer of mine for you all making request with joy, <hi type="super">5</hi> For your fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now; <hi type="super">6</hi> Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform <hi type="italic">it</hi> until the day of Jesus Christ: <div eID="gen31916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31917" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds after the inscription and benediction to thanksgiving for the saints at Philippi. He tells them what it was he thanked God for, upon their account. Observe here, <div eID="gen31917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31918" type="x-p"/> I. Paul remembered them: he bore them much in his thoughts; and though they were out of sight, and he was at a distance from them, yet they were not out of his mind: or, <hi type="italic">Upon every mention of you</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi pase te mneia.</hi></hi> As he often thought of them, so he often spoke of them, and delighted to hear them spoken of. The very mention of them was grateful to him: it is a pleasure to hear of the welfare of an absent friend. <div eID="gen31918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31919" type="x-p"/> II. He remembered them with joy. At Philippi he was maltreated; there he was scourged and put into the stocks, and for the present saw little of the fruit of his labour; and yet he remembers Philippi with joy. He looked upon his sufferings for Christ as his credit, his comfort, his crown, and was pleased at every mention of the place where he suffered. So far was he from being ashamed of them, or loth to hear of the scene of his sufferings, that he remembered it with joy. <div eID="gen31919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31920" type="x-p"/> III. He remembered them in prayer: <hi type="italic">Always in every prayer of mine for you all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.4">v. 4</reference>. The best remembrance of our friends is to remember them at the throne of grace. Paul was much in prayer for his friends, for all his friends, for these particularly. It should seem, by this manner of expression, that he mentioned at the throne of grace the several churches he was interested in and concerned for particularly and by name. He had seasons of prayer for the church at Philippi. God gives us leave to be thus free with him, though, for our comfort, he knows whom we mean when we do not name them. <div eID="gen31920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31921" type="x-p"/> IV. He thanked God upon every joyful remembrance of them. Observe, Thanksgiving must have a part in every prayer; and whatsoever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving. What we have the comfort of, God must have the glory of. He thanked God, as well as made requests with joy. As holy joy is the heart and soul of thankful praise, so thankful praise is the lip and language of holy joy. <div eID="gen31921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31922" type="x-p"/> V. As in our prayers, so in our thanksgiving, we must eye God as our God: <hi type="italic">I thank my God.</hi> It encourages us in prayer, and enlarges the heart in praise, to see every mercy coming from the hand of God as our God.—<hi type="italic">I thank my God upon every remembrance of you.</hi> We must thank our God for others' graces and comforts, and gifts and usefulness, as we receive the benefit of them, and God receives glory by them. But what is the matter of this thanksgiving? 1. He gives thanks to God for the comfort he had in them: for <hi type="italic">your fellowship in the gospel, from the first day until now,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe, Gospel fellowship is a good fellowship; and the meanest Christians have fellowship in the gospel with the greatest apostles, for the gospel salvation is a <hi type="italic">common salvation</hi> ( <reference osisRef="Jude.1.3">Jude 3</reference>), and they <hi type="italic">obtain like precious faith</hi> with them, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.1">2 Pet. i. 1</reference>. Those who sincerely receive and embrace the gospel have fellowship in it <hi type="italic">from the very first day:</hi> a new-born Christian, if he is true-born, is interested in all the promises and privileges of the gospel from the first day of his becoming such.—<hi type="italic">Until now.</hi> Observe, It is a great comfort to ministers when those who begin well hold on and persevere. Some, by their <hi type="italic">fellowship in the gospel,</hi> understand their liberality towards propagating the gospel, and translate <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">koinonia,</hi></hi> not <hi type="italic">communion,</hi> but <hi type="italic">communication.</hi> But, comparing it with Paul's thanksgiving on the account of other churches, it rather seems to be taken more generally for the fellowship which they had, in faith, and hope, and holy love, with all good Christians—a fellowship in gospel promises, ordinances, privileges, and hopes; and this from the <hi type="italic">first day until now.</hi> 2. For the confidence he had concerning them (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Being confident of this very thing,</hi> &c. Observe, The confidence of Christians is the great comfort of Christians, and we may fetch matter of praise from our hopes as well as from our joys; we must give thanks not only for what we have the present possession and evidence of, but for what we have the future prospect of. Paul speaks with much confidence concerning the good estate of others, hoping well concerning them in the judgment of charity, and being confident in the judgment of faith that if they were sincere they would be happy: <hi type="italic">That he who has begun a good work in you will perform it unto the day of Jesus Christ.</hi> A good work <hi type="italic">among you</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en hymin,</hi></hi> so it may be read: understand it, in the general, of the planting of the church among them. He who hath planted Christianity in the world will preserve it as long as the world stands. Christ will have a church till the mystery of God shall be finished and the mystical body completed. The church is built upon a rock, and the <hi type="italic">gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</hi> But it is rather to be applied to particular persons, and then it speaks of the certain accomplishment of the work of grace wherever it is begun. Observe here, (1.) The work of grace is a good work, a blessed work; for it makes us good, and is an earnest of good to us. It makes us like God, and fits us for the enjoyment of God. That may well be called a good work which does us the greatest good. (2.) Wherever this good work is begun it is of God's beginning: <hi type="italic">He has begun a good work in you.</hi> We could not begin it ourselves, for we are by nature <hi type="italic">dead in trespasses and sins:</hi> and what can dead men do towards raising themselves to life; or how can they begin to act till they are enlivened in the same respect in which they are said to be dead? It is God who quickens those who are thus dead, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Eph. ii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.13">Col. ii. 13</reference>. (3.) The work of grace is but begun in this life; it is not finished here; as long as we are in this imperfect state there is something more to be done. (4.) If the same God who begins the good work did not undertake the carrying on and finishing of it, it would lie for ever unfinished. He must perform it who began it. (5.) We may be confident, or well persuaded, that God not only will not forsake, but that he will finish and crown the work of his own hands. For, <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> (6.) The work of grace will never be perfected <hi type="italic">till the day of Jesus Christ,</hi> the day of his appearance. When he shall come to judge the world, and finish his mediation, then this work will be complete, and the top-stone will be brought forth with shouting. We have the same expression, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.10">v. 10</reference>.
entries.2dea5509074eebee066f971c3dc09e107335420a: <div eID="gen31922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Affection and Hope. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace. <hi type="super">8</hi> For God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen31923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31924" type="x-p"/> The apostle expresses the ardent affection he had for them, and his concern for their spiritual welfare: <hi type="italic">I have you in my heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.7">v. 7</reference>. He loved them as his own soul, and they lay near his heart. He thought much of them, and was in care about them. Observe, 1. Why he had them in his heart: <hi type="italic">Inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, you all are partakers of my grace;</hi> that is, they had received benefit by him and by his ministry; they were partakers of that grace of God which by him, and through his hands, was communicated to them. This makes people dear to their ministers—their receiving benefit by their ministry. Or, "<hi type="italic">You are partakers of my grace,</hi> you have joined with me in doing and suffering." They were partakers of his affliction by sympathy and concern, and readiness to assist him. Thus he calls being partakers of his grace; for those who suffer with the saints are and shall be comforted with them; and those shall share in the reward, who bear their part of the burden. He loved them because they adhered to him in his bonds, and in the <hi type="italic">defence and confirmation of the gospel:</hi> they were as ready to appear in their places, and according to their capacity, for the defence of the gospel, as the apostle was in his; and therefore he had them in his heart. Fellow sufferers should be dear one to another; those who have ventured and suffered in the same good cause of God and religion should for that reason love one another dearly: or, because <hi type="italic">you have me at heart</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dia to echein me en te kardia hymas.</hi></hi> They manifested their respect for him by adhering firmly to the doctrine he preached, and readily suffering for it along with him. The truest mark of respect towards our ministers is receiving and abiding by the doctrine they preach. 2. The evidence of it: <hi type="italic">It is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart.</hi> By this it appeared that he had them in his heart, because he had a good opinion of them and good hopes concerning them. Observe, It is very proper to think the best of other people, and as well as we can of them—to suppose as well of them as the matter will admit in all cases. 3. An appeal to God concerning the truth of this (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">For God is my record how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ.</hi> Having them in his heart, he longed after them; either he longed to see them, longed to hear from them, or he longed for their spiritual welfare and their increase and improvement in knowledge and grace. He had <hi type="italic">joy in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.4">v. 4</reference>), because of the good he saw and heard of among them; yet still he longed after them, to hear of more of it among them; and he <hi type="italic">longed after them all,</hi> not only those among them who were witty and wealthy, but even the meanest and poorest; and he <hi type="italic">longed greatly</hi> after them, or with strong affection and great good-will; and this <hi type="italic">in the bowels of Jesus Christ,</hi> with that tender concern which Christ himself has and has shown to precious souls. Paul was herein a follower of Christ, and all good ministers should aim to be so. O the bowels of compassion which are in Jesus Christ to poor souls! It was in compassion to them that he undertook their salvation, and put himself to so vast an expense to compass it. Now, in conformity to the example of Christ, Paul had a compassion for them, and longed after them all <hi type="italic">in the bowels of Jesus Christ.</hi> Shall not we pity and love those souls whom Christ had such a love and pity for? For this he appeals to God: <hi type="italic">God is my record.</hi> It was an inward disposition of mind that he expressed towards them, to the sincerity of which God only was witness, and therefore to him he appeals. "Whether you know it or not, or are sensible of it, God, who knows the heart, knows it."
entries.262ddcb8b8d17294a344973de9ff756a28cc93ce: <div eID="gen31924" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Affection and Hope. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31925" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and <hi type="italic">in</hi> all judgment; <hi type="super">10</hi> That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ; <hi type="super">11</hi> Being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are by Jesus Christ, unto the glory and praise of God. <div eID="gen31925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31926" type="x-p"/> These verses contain the prayers he put up for them. Paul often let his friends know what it was he begged of God for them, that they might know what to beg for themselves and be directed in their own prayers, and that they might be encouraged to hope they should receive from God the quickening, strengthening, everlasting, comforting grace, which so powerful an intercessor as Paul asked of God for them. It is an encouragement to us to know that we are prayed for by our friends, who, we have reason to think, have an interest at the throne of grace. It was intended likewise for their direction in their walk, and that they might labour to answer his prayers for them; for by this it would appear that God had answered them. Paul, in praying thus for them, expected good concerning them. It is an inducement to us to do our duty, that we may not disappoint the expectations of praying friends and ministers. He prayed, 1. That they might be a loving people, and that good affections might abound among them; <hi type="italic">That your love might abound yet more and more.</hi> He means it of their love to God, and one another, and all men. Love is the fulfilling both of the law and of the gospel. Observe, Those who abound much in any grace have still need to abound more and more, because there is still something wanting in it and we are imperfect in our best attainments. 2. That they might be a knowing and judicious people: that love might abound <hi type="italic">in knowledge and in all judgment.</hi> It is not a blind love that will recommend us to God, but a love grounded upon knowledge and judgment. We must love God because of his infinite excellence and loveliness, and love our brethren because of what we see of the image of God upon them. Strong passions, without knowledge and a settled judgment, will not make us complete in the will of God, and sometimes do more hurt than good. The Jews had a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, and were transported by it to violence and rage, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Rom. x. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.2">John xvi. 2</reference>. 3. That they might be a discerning people. This would be the effect of their knowledge and judgment: <hi type="italic">That you may approve the things which are excellent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.10">v. 10</reference>); or, as it is in the margin, <hi type="italic">Try the things which differ;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis to dokimazein humas ta diapheronta,</hi></hi> that we may approve the things which are excellent upon the trial of them, and discern their difference from other things. Observe, The truths and laws of Christ are excellent things; and it is necessary that we every one approve them, and esteem them such. We only need to try them, to approve of them; and they will easily recommend themselves to any searching and discerning mind. 4. That they might be an honest upright-hearted people: <hi type="italic">That you may be sincere.</hi> Sincerity is our gospel perfection, that in which we should have our conversation in the world, and which is the glory of all our graces. When the eye is single, when we are inward with God in what we do, are really what we appear to be, and mean honestly, then we are sincere. 5. That they might be an inoffensive people: that you may be <hi type="italic">without offence until the day of Christ;</hi> not apt to take offence; and very careful not to give offence to God or their brethren, to <hi type="italic">live in all good conscience before God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.1">Acts xxiii. 1</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">exercise ourselves to have always a conscience void of offence towards God and towards men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Acts xxiv. 16</reference>. And we must continue to the end <hi type="italic">blameless,</hi> that we may be presented so at the <hi type="italic">day of Christ.</hi> He will present the church <hi type="italic">without spot or wrinkle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Eph. v. 27</reference>), and <hi type="italic">present</hi> believers <hi type="italic">faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.24">Jude 24</reference>. 6. That they might be a fruitful useful people (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Being filled with the fruits of righteousness,</hi> &c. From God is our fruit found, and therefore from him it must be asked. The <hi type="italic">fruits of righteousness</hi> are the evidences and effects of our sanctification, the duties of holiness springing from a renewed heart, the <hi type="italic">root of the matter in us. Being filled</hi> with them. Observe, Those who do much good should still endeavour to do more. The fruits of righteousness, brought forth for the glory of God and edification of his church, should really fill us, and wholly take us up. Fear not being emptied by bringing forth the fruits of righteousness, for you will be filled with them. These fruits are <hi type="italic">by Jesus Christ,</hi> by his strength and grace, for <hi type="italic">without him we can do nothing.</hi> He is the root of the good olive, from which it derives its fatness. We are <hi type="italic">strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">2 Tim. ii. 1</reference>) and <hi type="italic">strengthened with might by his Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Eph. iii. 16</reference>), and they are <hi type="italic">unto the glory and praise of God.</hi> We must not aim at our own glory in our fruitfulness, but at the <hi type="italic">praise and glory of God,</hi> that <hi type="italic">God may be glorified in all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Peter iv. 11</reference>), and <hi type="italic">whatsoever we do we must do all to the glory of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1 Cor. x. 31</reference>. It is much for the honour of God, when Christians not only are good, but do good, and <hi type="italic">abound in good works.</hi>
entries.1b48ec7721211eefa420eb45853b76374a775636: <div eID="gen31926" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Success and Joy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31927" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things <hi type="italic">which happened</hi> unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel; <hi type="super">13</hi> So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other <hi type="italic">places;</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And many of the brethren in the Lord, waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear. <hi type="super">15</hi> Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: <hi type="super">16</hi> The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: <hi type="super">17</hi> But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. <hi type="super">18</hi> What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice. <hi type="super">19</hi> For I know that this shall turn to my salvation through your prayer, and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, <hi type="super">20</hi> According to my earnest expectation and <hi type="italic">my</hi> hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but <hi type="italic">that</hi> with all boldness, as always, <hi type="italic">so</hi> now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> by life, or by death. <div eID="gen31927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31928" type="x-p"/> We see here the care the apostle takes to prevent their being offended at his sufferings. He was now a prisoner at Rome; this might be a stumbling-block to those who had received the gospel by his ministry. They might be tempted to think, If this doctrine were indeed of God, God would not suffer one who was so active and instrumental in preaching and propagating it to be thrown by as a despised broken vessel. They might be shy of owning this doctrine, lest they should be involved in the same trouble themselves. Now to take off the offence of the cross, he expounds this dark and hard chapter of his sufferings, and makes it very easy and intelligible, and reconcilable to the wisdom and goodness of God who employed him. <div eID="gen31928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31929" type="x-p"/> I. He suffered by the sworn enemies of the gospel, who laid him in prison, and aimed at taking away his life; but they should not be stumbled at this, for good was brought out of it, and it tended to the furtherance of the gospel (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.</hi> A strange chemistry of Providence this, to extract so great a good as the enlargement of the gospel out of so great an evil as the confinement of the apostle. "<hi type="italic">I suffer trouble as an evil-doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2 Tim. ii. 9</reference>. They cannot imprison the word of God; that has its free course, though I am confined." But how was this? <div eID="gen31929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31930" type="x-p"/> 1. It alarmed those who were without (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My bonds in Christ,</hi> or for Christ, <hi type="italic">are manifest in all the palace and in all other places.</hi> The emperor, the courtiers, the magistrates, are convinced that I do not suffer as an evil-doer, but as an honest man, with a good conscience. They know that I suffer for Christ, and not for any wickedness." Observe, (1.) Paul's sufferings made him known at court, where perhaps he would never have otherwise been known; and this might lead some of them to enquire after the gospel for which he suffered, which they might otherwise have never heard of. (2.) When his bonds were manifest in the palace, they were manifest in all other places. <hi type="italic">The sentiments of the court have a great influence on the sentiments of all people—Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis.</hi> <div eID="gen31930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31931" type="x-p"/> 2. It emboldened those who were within. As his enemies were startled at his sufferings, so his friends were encouraged by them. <hi type="italic">Upright men shall be astonished at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite. The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he who has clean hands shall be stronger and stronger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.17.8-Job.17.9">Job xvii. 8, 9</reference>. So it was here: <hi type="italic">Many of the brethren in the Lord waxing confident by my bonds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.14">v. 14</reference>. The expectation of trouble for their religion, in general, perhaps disheartened and discouraged them; but, when they saw Paul imprisoned for Christ, they were so far from being deterred from preaching Christ and praising his name, that it made them the more bold; for they could gladly suffer in Paul's company. If they should be hurried from the pulpit to the prison, they could be reconciled to it, because they would be there in such good company. Besides, the comfort which Paul had in his sufferings, his extraordinary consolations received from Christ in a suffering state, greatly encouraged them. They saw that those who served Christ served a good Master, who could both bear them up and bear them out, in their sufferings for him. <hi type="italic">Waxing confident by my bonds.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Pepoithotas.</hi></hi> They were more fully satisfied and persuaded by what they saw. Observe the power of divine grace; that which was intended by the enemy to discourage the preachers of the gospel was overruled for their encouragement. And <hi type="italic">are much more bold to speak the word without fear;</hi> they see the worst of it, and therefore are not afraid to venture. Their confidence gave them courage, and their courage preserved them from the power of fear. <div eID="gen31931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31932" type="x-p"/> II. He suffered from false friends as well as from enemies (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.15-Phil.1.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Some preach Christ even of envy and strife. The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely.</hi> Now this would be a stumbling-block and discouragement to some, that there were those who envied Paul's reputation in the churches, and the interest he had among the Christians, and endeavoured to supplant and undermine him. They were secretly pleased when he was laid up in prison, that they might have the better opportunity to steal away the people's affections; and they laid themselves out the more in preaching, that they might gain to themselves the reputation they envied him: <hi type="italic">Supposing to add affliction to my bonds.</hi> They thought hereby to grieve his spirit, and make him afraid of losing his interest, uneasy under his confinement, and impatient for release. It is sad that there should be men who profess the gospel, especially who preach it, who are governed by such principles as these, who should preach Christ in spite to Paul, and to increase the affliction of his bonds. Let us not think it strange if in these later and more degenerate ages of the church there should be any such. However, there were others who were animated by Paul's sufferings to preach Christ the more vigorously: <hi type="italic">Some also of good will, and love:</hi> from sincere affection to the gospel, that the work might not stand while the workman was laid up.—<hi type="italic">Knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel.</hi> They knew that he was appointed to support and propagate the gospel in the world, against all the violence and opposition of its enemies, and were afraid lest the gospel should suffer by his confinement. This made them the more bold to preach the word and <hi type="italic">supply his lack of service</hi> to the church. <div eID="gen31932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31933" type="x-p"/> III. It is very affecting to see how easy he was in the midst of all: <hi type="italic">Notwithstanding every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and I will rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">v. 18</reference>. Note, The preaching of Christ is the joy of all who wish well to his kingdom among men. Since it may tend to the good of many, we ought to rejoice in it, though it be done in pretence, and not in reality. It is God's prerogative to judge of the principles men act upon; this is out of our line. Paul was so far from envying those who had liberty to preach the gospel while he was under confinement that he rejoiced in the preaching of it even by those who do it in pretence, and not in truth. How much more then should we rejoice in the preaching of the gospel by those who do it in truth, yea, though it should be with much weakness and some mistake! Two things made the apostle rejoice in the preaching of the gospel:— <div eID="gen31933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31934" type="x-p"/> 1. Because it tended to the salvation of the souls of men: <hi type="italic">I know that this shall turn to my salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.19">v. 19</reference>. Observe, God can bring good out of evil; and what does not turn to the salvation of the ministers may yet, by the grace of God, be made to turn to the salvation of the people. What reward can those expect who preach Christ out <hi type="italic">of strife, and envy, and contention,</hi> and to add affliction to a faithful minister's bonds? who preach in pretence, and not in truth? And yet even this may turn to the salvation of others; and Paul's rejoicing in it turned to his salvation too. This is one of the things which <hi type="italic">accompany salvation</hi>—to be able to rejoice that Christ is preached, though it be to the diminution of us and our reputation. This noble spirit appeared in John the Baptist, at the first public preaching of Christ: "<hi type="italic">This my joy therefore is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.29-John.3.30">John iii. 29, 30</reference>. Let him shine, though I be obscured; and his glory be exalted, though upon my ruins." Others understand this expression of the malice of his enemies being defeated, and contributing towards his deliverance from his confinement. <hi type="italic">Through your prayers, and the supply of the Spirit of Christ.</hi> Note, Whatever turns to our salvation is by the supply or the aids and assistance of the Spirit of Christ; and prayer is the appointed means of fetching in that supply. The prayers of the people may bring a supply of the Spirit to their ministers, to support them in suffering, as well as in preaching the gospel. <div eID="gen31934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31935" type="x-p"/> 2. Because it would turn to the glory of Christ, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.20">v. 20</reference>, where he takes occasion to mention his own entire devotedness to the service and honour of Christ: <hi type="italic">According to my earnest expectation and hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed,</hi> &c. Here observe, (1.) The great desire of every true Christian is that Christ may be magnified and glorified, that his name may be great, and his kingdom come. (2.) Those who truly desire that Christ may be magnified desire that he may be <hi type="italic">magnified in their body.</hi> They present their <hi type="italic">bodies a living sacrifice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Rom. xii. 1</reference>), and <hi type="italic">yield their members as instruments of righteousness unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.13">Rom. vi. 13</reference>. They are willing to serve his designs, and be instrumental to his glory, with every member of their body, as well as faculty of their soul. (3.) It is much for the glory of Christ that we should serve him boldly and not be ashamed of him, with freedom and liberty of mind, and without discouragement: <hi type="italic">That in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness Christ may be magnified.</hi> The boldness of Christians is the honour of Christ. (4.) Those who make Christ's glory their desire and design may make it their expectation and hope. If it be truly aimed at, it shall certainly be attained. If in sincerity we pray, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> we may be sure of the same answer to that prayer which Christ had: <hi type="italic">I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.28">John xii. 28</reference>. (5.) Those who desire that Christ may be magnified in their bodies have a holy indifference <hi type="italic">whether it be by life or by death.</hi> They refer it to him which way he will make them serviceable to his glory, whether by their labours or sufferings, by their diligence or patience, by their living to his honour in working for him or dying to his honour in suffering for him.
entries.b1a492e1ded6b7853a74e9eeba43b6f438159991: <div eID="gen31935" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Generous Exultation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31936" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> For to me to live <hi type="italic">is</hi> Christ, and to die <hi type="italic">is</hi> gain. <hi type="super">22</hi> But if I live in the flesh, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not. <hi type="super">23</hi> For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: <hi type="super">24</hi> Nevertheless to abide in the flesh <hi type="italic">is</hi> more needful for you. 25 And having this confidence, I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith; <hi type="super">26</hi> That your rejoicing may be more abundant in Jesus Christ for me by my coming to you again. <div eID="gen31936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31937" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the life and death of blessed Paul: his life was Christ, and his death was gain. Observe, 1. It is the undoubted character of every good Christian that to him to live is Christ. The glory of Christ ought to be the end of our life, the grace of Christ the principle of our life, and the word of Christ the rule of it. The Christian life is derived from Christ, and directed to him. He is the principle, rule, and end of it. 2. All those to whom to live is Christ to them to die <hi type="italic">will be gain:</hi> it is great gain, a present gain, everlasting gain. Death is a great loss to a carnal worldly man; for he loses all his comforts and all his hopes: but to a good Christian it is gain, for it is the end of all his weakness and misery and the perfection of his comforts and accomplishment of his hopes; it delivers him from all the evils of life, and brings him to the possession of the chief good. Or, <hi type="italic">To me to die is gain;</hi> that is, "to the gospel as well as to myself, which will receive a further confirmation by the seal of my blood, as it had before by the labours of my life." So Christ would be <hi type="italic">magnified by his death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.20">v. 20</reference>. Some read the whole expression thus: <hi type="italic">To me, living and dying, Christ is gain;</hi> that is, "I desire no more, neither while I live nor when I die, but to win Christ and be found in him." It might be thought, if death were gain to him, he would be weary of life, and impatient for death. No, says he, <div eID="gen31937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31938" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">If I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.22">v. 22</reference>), that is, Christ is. He reckoned his labour well bestowed, if he could be instrumental to advance the honour and interest of the kingdom of Christ in the world. It is <hi type="italic">the fruit of my labour</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">karpos ergou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">operæ pretium.</hi> It is worth while for a good Christian and a good minister to live in the world as long as he can glorify God and do good to his church. <hi type="italic">Yet what I shall choose I wot not; for I am in a strait betwixt two.</hi> It was a blessed strait which Paul was in, not between two evil things, but between two good things. David was in a strait by three judgments—sword, famine, and pestilence: Paul was in a strait between two blessings—living to Christ, and being with him. Here we have him reasoning with himself upon the matter. <div eID="gen31938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31939" type="x-p"/> 1. His inclination was for death. See the power of faith and of divine grace; it can reconcile the mind to death, and make us willing to die, though death is the destruction of our present nature and the greatest natural evil. We have naturally an aversion to death, but he had an inclination to it (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">v. 23</reference>); <hi type="italic">Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ,</hi> Observe, (1.) It is being with Christ which makes a departure desirable to a good man. It is not simply dying, or putting off the body, it is not of itself and for its own sake a desirable thing; but it may be necessarily connected with something else which may make it truly so. If I cannot be with Christ without departing, I shall reckon it desirable on that account to depart. (2.) As soon as ever the soul departs, it is immediately with Christ. <hi type="italic">This day shalt thou be with me in paradise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.43">Luke xxiii. 43</reference>. <hi type="italic">Absent from the body and present with the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">2 Cor. v. 8</reference>), without any interval between. <hi type="italic">Which is far better,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pollo gar mallon kreisson</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">very much exceeding,</hi> or <hi type="italic">vastly preferable.</hi> Those who know the value of Christ and heaven will readily acknowledge it far better to be in heaven than to be in this world, to be with Christ than to be with any creature; for in this world we are compassed about with sin, born to trouble, born again to it; but, if we come to be with Christ, farewell sin and temptation, farewell sorrow and death, for ever. <div eID="gen31939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31940" type="x-p"/> 2. His judgment was rather to live awhile longer in this world, for the service of the church (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.</hi> It is needful for the church to have ministers; and faithful ministers can ill be spared when the <hi type="italic">harvest is plenteous and the labourers are few.</hi> Observe, Those who have most reason to desire to depart should be willing to continue in the world as long as God has any work for them to do. Paul's strait was not between living in this world and living in heaven; between these two there is no comparison: but his strait was between serving Christ in this world and enjoying him in another. Still it was Christ that his heart was upon: though, to advance the interest of Christ and his church, he chose rather to tarry here, where he met with oppositions and difficulties, and to deny himself for awhile the satisfaction of his reward. <div eID="gen31940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31941" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">And, having this confidence, I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.25">v. 25</reference>. Observe here, 1. What a great confidence Paul had in the divine Providence, that it would order all for the best to him. "Having this confidence that it will be needful for you that I should abide in the flesh, I know that I shall abide." 2. Whatsoever is best for the church, we may be sure God will do. If we know what is needful for building up the body of Christ, we may certainly know what will be; for he will take care of its interests, and do what is best, all things considered, in every condition it is in. 3. Observe what ministers are continued for: <hi type="italic">For our furtherance and joy of faith,</hi> our further advancement in holiness and comfort. 4. What promotes our <hi type="italic">faith and joy of faith</hi> is very much for our furtherance in the way to heaven. The more faith the more joy, and the more faith and joy the more we are furthered in our Christian course. 5. There is need of a settled ministry, not only for the conviction and conversion of sinners, but for the edification of saints, and their furtherance in spiritual attainments. <div eID="gen31941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31942" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">That your rejoicing may be more abundant in Jesus Christ for me, by my coming to you again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.26">v. 26</reference>. They rejoiced in the hope of seeing him, and enjoying his further labours among them. Observe, 1. The continuance of ministers with the church ought to be the rejoicing of all who wish well to the church, and to its interests. 2. All our joys should terminate in Christ. Our joy in good ministers should be our joy <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus for them;</hi> for they are but the <hi type="italic">friends of the bridegroom,</hi> and are to be received in his name, and for his sake.
entries.0ddaacee4eaba553e549c4a791c9ed3388bc00f4: <div eID="gen31942" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31943" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel; <hi type="super">28</hi> And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God. <hi type="super">29</hi> For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake; <hi type="super">30</hi> Having the same conflict which ye saw in me, and now hear <hi type="italic">to be</hi> in me. <div eID="gen31943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31944" type="x-p"/> The apostle concludes the chapter with two exhortations:— <div eID="gen31944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31945" type="x-p"/> I. He exhorts them to strictness of conversation (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Only let your conversation be as becometh the gospel of Christ.</hi> Observe, Those who profess the gospel of Christ should have their conversation as becomes the gospel, or in a suitableness and agreeableness to it. Let it be as becomes those who believe gospel truths, submit to gospel laws, and depend upon gospel promises; and with an answerable faith, holiness, and comfort. Let it be in all respects as those who belong to the kingdom of God among men, and are members and subjects of it. It is an ornament to our profession when our conversation is of a piece with it.—<hi type="italic">That whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs.</hi> He had spoken in <reference osisRef="Phil.1.26">v. 26</reference> of his coming to them again, and had spoken it with some assurance, though he was now a prisoner; but he would not have them build upon that. Our religion must not be bound up in the hands of our ministers: "Whether I come or no, let me hear well of you, and do you stand fast." Whether ministers come or no, Christ is always at hand. He is nigh to us, never far from us; and hastens his second coming. <hi type="italic">The coming of the Lord draws nigh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.8">James v. 8</reference>. Let me hear of you <hi type="italic">that you stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel.</hi> Three things he desired to hear of them; and they are all such as become the gospel:—1. It becomes those who profess the gospel to strive for it, to use a holy violence in taking the kingdom of heaven. The <hi type="italic">faith of the gospel</hi> is the doctrine of faith, <hi type="italic">or</hi> the religion of the gospel. There is that in the faith of the gospel which is worth striving for. If religion is worth any thing, it is worth every thing. There is much opposition, and there is need of striving. A man may sleep and go to hell; but he who will go to heaven must look about him and be diligent. 2. The unity and unanimity of Christians become the gospel: <hi type="italic">Strive together,</hi> not strive one with another; all of you must strive against the common adversary. One spirit and one mind become the gospel; for <hi type="italic">there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism.</hi> There may be a oneness of heart and affection among Christians, where there is diversity of judgment and apprehensions about many things. 3. Stedfastness becomes the gospel: <hi type="italic">Stand fast in one spirit, with one mind.</hi> Be <hi type="italic">stedfast and immovable</hi> by any opposition. It is a shame to religion when the professors of it are off and on, unfixed in their minds, and unstable as water; for they will never excel. Those who would strive for the faith of the gospel must stand firm to it. <div eID="gen31945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31946" type="x-p"/> II. He exhorts them to courage and constancy in suffering: <hi type="italic">And in nothing terrified by your adversaries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.28">v. 28</reference>. The professors of the gospel have all along met with adversaries, especially at the first planting of Christianity. Our great care must be to keep close to our profession, and be constant to it: whatever oppositions we meet with, we must not be frightened at them, considering that the condition of the persecuted is much better and more desirable than the condition of the persecutors; for persecuting is an <hi type="italic">evident token of perdition.</hi> Those who oppose the gospel of Christ, and injure the professors of it, are marked out for ruin. But being persecuted is a token of salvation. Not that it is a certain mark; many hypocrites have suffered for their religion; but it is a good sign that we are in good earnest in religion, and designed for salvation, when we are enabled in a right manner to suffer for the cause of Christ.—<hi type="italic">For to you it is given on the behalf of Christ not only to believe, but also to suffer for his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">v. 29</reference>. Here are two precious gifts given, and both on the behalf of Christ:—1. To believe in him. Faith is God's gift on the behalf of Christ, who purchased for us not only the blessedness which is the object of faith, but the grace of faith itself: the ability or disposition to believe is from God. 2. To suffer for the sake of Christ is a valuable gift too: it is a great honour and a great advantage; for we may be very serviceable to the glory of God, which is the end of our creation, and encourage and confirm the faith of others. And there is a great reward attending it too: <hi type="italic">Blessed are you when men shall persecute you, for great is your reward in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.11-Matt.5.12">Matt. v. 11, 12</reference>. And, if <hi type="italic">we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2 Tim. ii. 12</reference>. If we suffer reproach and loss for Christ, we are to reckon it a great gift, and prize it accordingly, always provided we behave under our sufferings with the genuine temper of martyrs and confessors (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Having the same conflict which you saw in me, and now hear to be in me;</hi> that is, suffering in the same manner as you saw and now hear of me that I suffer." It is not simply the suffering, but the cause, and not only the cause, but the spirit, which makes the martyr. A man may suffer in a bad cause, and then he suffers justly; or in a good cause, but with a wrong mind, and then his sufferings lose their value.  <chapter eID="Phil.1"/> <div eID="gen31946" type="x-p"/>

entries.2aa081ea0f970b6a6bbe5a145f50ff5ab5f2ff76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17724"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen35866" type="x-p"/> The INTERNAL EVIDENCE for the authenticity of this Epistle is strong. The style, manner of thought, and doctrine, accord with Paul's. The incidental allusions also establish his authorship. Paley [Horæ Paulinæ, ch. 7] instances the mention of the object of Epaphroditus' journey to Rome, the Philippian contribution to Paul's wants, Epaphroditus' sickness (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.7">Php 1:7</reference>; 2:25-30; 4:10-18), the fact that Timothy had been long with Paul at Philippi (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>; 2:19), the reference to his being a prisoner at Rome now for a long time (Php 1:12-14; 2:17-28), his willingness to die (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Php 1:23</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">2Co 5:8</reference>), the reference to the Philippians having seen his maltreatment at Philippi (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Php 1:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2:1, 2</reference>).<div eID="gen35866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35867" type="x-p"/> The EXTERNAL EVIDENCE is equally decisive: Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 3; 11]; Irenæus [Against Heresies, 4.18.4]; Clement of Alexandria [The Instructor, 1.1, p. 107]; Eusebius [The Epistle of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne, in Ecclesiastical History, 5. 2]; Tertullian [On the Resurrection of the Flesh, 23]; Origen [Against Celsus, 1.3, p. 122]; Cyprian [Testimonies against the Jews, 3.39].<div eID="gen35867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35868" type="x-p"/> Philippi was the first (that is, the farthest from Rome, and first which met Paul in entering Macedonia) Macedonian city of the district, called Macedonia Prima (so called as lying farthest eastward). The Greek (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">Ac 16:12</reference>) should not be translated "the chief city," as English Version, but as above [Alford]. Not it, but Thessalonica, was the chief city of the province, and Amphipolis, of the district called Macedonia Prima. It was a Roman "colony" (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">Ac 16:12</reference>), made so by Augustus, to commemorate his famous victory over Brutus and Cassius. A colony was in fact a portion of Rome itself transplanted to the provinces, an offshoot from Rome, and as it were a portrait of the mother city on a small scale [Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, 16.13]. Its inhabitants were Roman citizens, having the right of voting in the Roman tribes, governed by their own senate and magistrates, and not by the governor of the province, with the Roman law and Latin language.<div eID="gen35868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35869" type="x-p"/> Paul, with Silas and Timothy, planted the Gospel there (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">Ac 16:12</reference>, &c.), in his second missionary journey, A.D. 51. Doubtless he visited it again on his journey from Ephesus into Macedonia (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">Ac 20:1</reference>); and <reference osisRef="Acts.20.3">Ac 20:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">6</reference>, expressly mentions his third visit on his return from Greece (Corinth) to Syria by way of Macedonia. His sufferings at Philippi (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.19">Ac 16:19</reference>, &c.) strengthened the Christian bond of union between him and his Philippian converts, who also, like him, were exposed to trials for the Gospel's sake (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>). They alone sent supplies for his temporal wants, twice shortly after he had left them (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>), and again a third time shortly before writing this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.10">Php 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>). This fervent attachment on their part was, perhaps, also in part due to the fact that few Jews were in Philippi, as in other scenes of his labors, to sow the seeds of distrust and suspicion. There was no synagogue, but merely a Jewish Proseucha, or oratory, by the riverside. So that there only do we read of his meeting no opposition from Jews, but only from the masters of the divining damsel, whose gains had been put an end to by her being dispossessed.<div eID="gen35869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35870" type="x-p"/> Though the Philippian Church was as yet free from Judaizing influence, yet it needed to be forewarned of that danger which might at any time assail it from without (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Php 3:2</reference>); even as such evil influences had crept into the Galatian churches. In <reference osisRef="Phil.4.2">Php 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">3</reference> we find a trace of the fact recorded in the history (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.13">Ac 16:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.14">14</reference>), that female converts were among the first to receive the Gospel at Philippi.<div eID="gen35870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35871" type="x-p"/> As to the state of the Church, we gather from <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">2Co 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">2</reference> that its members were poor, yet most liberal; and from <reference osisRef="Phil.1.28-Phil.1.30">Php 1:28-30</reference>, that they were undergoing persecution. The only blemish referred to in their character was, on the part of some members, a tendency to dissension. Hence arise his admonitions against disputings (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">Php 1:27</reference>; 2:<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.12">1-4, 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen35871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35872" type="x-p"/> The OBJECT of the Epistle is general: not only to thank the Philippians for their contribution sent by Epaphroditus, who was now in returning to take back the apostle's letter, but to express his Christian love and sympathy, and to exhort them to a life consonant with that of Christ, and to warn them against existing dissensions and future possible assaults of Judaizers from without. It is remarkable in this Epistle alone, as compared with the others, that, amidst many commendations, there are no express censures of those to whom it is addressed. No doctrinal error, or schism, has as yet sprung up; the only blemish hinted at is, that some of the Philippian Church were somewhat wanting in lowliness of mind, the result of which want was disputation. Two women, Euodias and Syntyche, are mentioned as having erred in this respect (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.2">Php 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">3</reference>). The Epistle may be divided into three parts: (1) Affectionate address to the Philippians; reference to his own state as a prisoner at Rome, and to theirs, and to his mission of Epaphroditus to them (the first and second chapters). Epaphroditus probably held a leading office in the Philippian Church, perhaps as a presbyter. After Tychicus and Onesimus had departed (A.D. 62), carrying the Epistles to the Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon, Paul was cheered in his imprisonment by the arrival of Epaphroditus with the Philippian contribution. That faithful "brother, companion in labor, and fellow soldier" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.25">Php 2:25</reference>), had brought on himself by the fatigues of the journey a dangerous sickness (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.26">Php 2:26</reference>, 30). But now that he was recovered, he "longed" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.26">Php 2:26</reference>) to return to his Philippian flock, and in person to relieve their anxiety on his behalf, in respect to his sickness; and the apostle gladly availed himself of the opportunity of writing to them a letter of grateful acknowledgments and Christian exhortations. (2) Caution against Judaizing teachers, supported by reference to his own former and present feeling towards Jewish legalism (Php 3:1-21). (3) Admonitions to individuals, and to the Church in general, thanks for their seasonable aid, and concluding benedictions and salutations (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.1-Phil.4.23">Php 4:1-23</reference>).<div eID="gen35872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35873" type="x-p"/> This Epistle was written from Rome during the imprisonment, the beginning of which is related in <reference osisRef="Acts.28.16">Ac 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">20, 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">31</reference>. The reference to "Cæsar's household" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.22">Php 4:22</reference>), and to the "palace" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.13">Php 1:13</reference>, Greek, "Prætorium," probably, the barrack of the Prætorian bodyguard, attached to the palace of Nero) confirms this. It must have been during his first imprisonment at Rome, for the mention of the Prætorium agrees with the fact that it was during his first imprisonment he was in the custody of the Prætorian Prefect, and his situation, described in <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12-Phil.1.14">Php 1:12-14</reference>, agrees with his situation in the first two years of his imprisonment (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.30">Ac 28:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.31">31</reference>). The following reasons show, moreover, that it was written towards the close of that imprisonment: (1) He, in it, expresses his expectation of the immediate decision of his cause (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.23">Php 2:23</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>) Enough time had elapsed for the Philippians to hear of his imprisonment, to send Epaphroditus to him, to hear of Epaphroditus' arrival and sickness, and send back word to Rome of their distress (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.26">Php 2:26</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>) It must have been written after the three other Epistles sent from Rome, namely, Colossians, Ephesians, and Philemon; for Luke is no longer with him (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.20">Php 2:20</reference>); otherwise he would have been specified as saluting them, having formerly labored among them, whereas he is mentioned as with him, <reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>; Phm 24. Again, in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference>, his freedom to preach is implied: but in <reference osisRef="Phil.1.13-Phil.1.18">Php 1:13-18</reference>, his bondage is dwelt on, and it is implied that, not himself, but others, preached, and made his imprisonment known. Again, in Phm 22, he confidently anticipates his release, which contrasts with the more depressed anticipations of this Epistle. (4) A considerable time had elapsed since the beginning of his imprisonment, for "his bonds" to have become so widely known, and to have produced such good effects for the Gospel (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.13">Php 1:13</reference>). (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>) There is evidently an increase in the rigor of his imprisonment implied now, as compared with the early stage of it, as described in <reference osisRef="Acts.28.1-Acts.28.31">Ac 28:1-31</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Php 1:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">30</reference>; 2:27. History furnishes a probable clue to account for this increase of vigor. In the second year of Paul's imprisonment (A.D. 62), Burrus, the Prætorian Prefect, to whose custody he had been committed (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.16">Ac 28:16</reference>, "the captain of the guard"), died; and Nero the emperor having divorced Octavia, and married Poppoea, a Jewish proselytess (who then caused her rival, Octavia, to be murdered, and gloated over the head of her victim), exalted Tigellinus, the chief promoter of the marriage, a monster of wickedness, to the Prætorian Prefecture. It was then he seems to have been removed from his own house into the Prætorium, or barrack of the Prætorian guards, attached to the palace, for stricter custody; and hence he writes with less hopeful anticipations as to the result of his trial (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Php 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>). Some of the Prætorian guards who had the custody of him before, would then naturally make known his "bonds," in accordance with <reference osisRef="Phil.1.13">Php 1:13</reference>; from the smaller Prætorian bodyguard at the palace the report would spread to the general permanent Prætorian camp, which Tiberius had established north of the city, outside of the walls. He had arrived in Rome, February, 61; the "two whole years (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">Ac 20:30</reference>) in his own hired house" ended February, 63, so that the date of this Epistle, written shortly after, evidently while the danger was imminent, would be about spring or summer, 63. The providence of God averted the danger. He probably was thought beneath the notice of Tigellinus, who was more intent on court intrigues. The death of Nero's favorite, Pallas, the brother of Felix, this same year, also took out of the way another source of danger.<div eID="gen35873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35874" type="x-p"/> The STYLE is abrupt and discontinuous, his fervor of affection leading him to pass rapidly from one theme to another (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.18">Php 2:18</reference>, 19-24, 25-30; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>, 2, 3, 4-14, 15). In no Epistle does he use so warm expressions of love. In <reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">Php 4:1</reference> he seems at a loss for words sufficient to express all the extent and ardor of his affection for the Philippians: "My brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved." The mention of bishops and deacons in <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference> is due to the late date of the Epistle, at a time when the Church had begun to assume that order which is laid down in the Pastoral Epistles, and which continued the prevalent one in the first and purest age of the Church.<div eID="gen35874" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Phil.1.1-Phil.1.30">Php 1:1-30</reference>. Inscription. Thanksgiving and Prayers for the Flourishing Spiritual State of the Philippians. His Own State at Rome, and the Result of His Imprisonment in Spreading the Gospel. Exhortation to Christian Consistency.</title> <div sID="gen35875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17724"/><hi type="bold">1. Timotheus--</hi>mentioned as being well known to the Philippians (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.3">Ac 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.10-Acts.16.12">10-12</reference>), and now present with Paul. Not that Timothy had any share in writing the Epistle; for Paul presently uses the first person singular, "I," not "we" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.3">Php 1:3</reference>). The mention of his name implies merely that Timothy joined in affectionate remembrances to them.<div eID="gen35875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">servants of Jesus Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the order, "Christ Jesus." Paul does not call himself "an apostle," as in the inscriptions of other Epistles; for the Philippians needed not to be reminded of his apostolic authority. He writes rather in a tone of affectionate familiarity.<div eID="gen35876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Phil.1.4">Php 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.8">7, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Php 2:17</reference>, 26. It implies comprehensive affection which desired not to forget any one among them "all."<div eID="gen35877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bishops--</hi>synonymous with "presbyters" in the apostolical churches; as appears from the same persons being called "elders of the Church" at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.17">Ac 20:17</reference>), and "overseers" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>), Greek, "bishops." And <reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>, compare with <reference osisRef="Phil.1.7">Php 1:7</reference>. This is the earliest letter of Paul where bishops and deacons are mentioned, and the only one where they are separately addressed in the salutation. This accords with the probable course of events, deduced alike from the letters and history. While the apostles were constantly visiting the churches in person or by messengers, regular pastors would be less needed; but when some were removed by various causes, provision for the permanent order of the churches would be needed. Hence the three pastoral letters, subsequent to this Epistle, give instruction as to the due appointment of bishops and deacons. It agrees with this new want of the Church, when other apostles were dead or far away, and Paul long in prison, that bishops and deacons should be prominent for the first time in the opening salutation. The Spirit thus intimated that the churches were to look up to their own pastors, now that the miraculous gifts were passing into God's ordinary providence, and the presence of the inspired apostles, the dispensers of those gifts, was to be withdrawn [Paley, "Horæ Paulinæ]. "Presbyter," implied the rank; "bishop," the duties of the office [Neander]. Naturally, when the apostles who had the chief supervision were no more, one among the presbyters presided and received the name "bishop," in the more restricted and modern sense; just as in the Jewish synagogue one of the elders presided as "ruler of the synagogue." Observe, the apostle addresses the Church (that is, the congregation) more directly than its presiding ministers (<reference osisRef="Col.4.17">Col 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">He 13:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>). The bishops managed more the internal, the deacons the external, affairs of the Church. The plural number shows there was more than one bishop or presbyter, and more than one deacon in the Church at Philippi. <div eID="gen35878" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c9be6199e9928585de9ea2c50841f257169092e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17725"/><div sID="gen35879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17725"/><hi type="bold">2. Grace ... peace--</hi>The very form of this salutation implies the union of Jew, Greek, and Roman. The Greek salutation was "joy" (chairein), akin to the Greek for "grace" (charis). The Roman was "health," the intermediate term between grace and peace. The Hebrew was "peace," including both temporal and spiritual prosperity. Grace must come first if we are to have true peace.<div eID="gen35879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ... from--</hi>Omit the second "from": as in the Greek, "God our Father" and "the Lord Jesus Christ," are most closely connected. <div eID="gen35880" type="x-p"/>
entries.a94174bfe297ce8140f47f406628c39bd5580dd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17726"/><div sID="gen35881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17726"/>3. Translate, "In all my remembrance of you." <div eID="gen35881" type="x-p"/>
entries.12b6a466fca5d2e3333a0c8327d63e70c6f8a65d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17727"/><div sID="gen35882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17727"/><hi type="bold">4. making request--</hi>Translate, "making my request."<div eID="gen35882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you all--</hi>The frequent repetition in this Epistle of "all" with "you," marks that Paul desires to declare his love for all alike, and will not recognize any divisions among them.<div eID="gen35883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with joy--</hi>the characteristic feature in this Epistle, as love is in that to the Ephesians (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Php 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.2">Php 2:2</reference>, 19, 28; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4</reference>). Love and joy are the two first-fruits of the Spirit. Joy gives especial animation to prayers. It marked his high opinion of them, that there was almost everything in them to give him joy, and almost nothing to give him pain. <div eID="gen35884" type="x-p"/>
