Interpreters have hitherto, in my opinion, given a wrong rendering and exposition to this passage; for they make this distinction, that Christ was life to Paul, and death was gain. I, on the other hand, make Christ the subject of discourse in both clauses, so that he is declared to be gain in him both in life and in death; for it is customary with the Greeks to leave the word πρός to be understood. Besides that this meaning is less forced, it also corresponds better with the foregoing statement, and contains more complete doctrine. He declares that it is indifferent to him, and is all one, whether he lives or dies, because, having Christ, he reckons both to be gain. And assuredly it is Christ alone that makes us happy both in death and in life; otherwise, if death is miserable, life is in no degree happier; so that it is difficult to determine whether it is more advantageous to live or to die out of Christ. On the other hand, let Christ be with us, and he will bless our life as well as our death, so that both will be happy and desirable for us.
Philippians 1:22-26
22. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not.
22. Quodsi vivere in carne operae pretium mihi est, etiam quid eligam ignoro.
“Or encore que viure en chair me fust proufitable, ie ne scay lequel ie doy eslire, ou, Or si viure en chair me est proufitable, et que c’est qu’ie doy eslire, ie ne scay rien;” — “But although to live in the flesh would not be profitable to me, I know not what I ought to choose; or, But if to live in the flesh is profitable to me, and that it is what I ought to choose, I know not.”
23. For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
23. Coarctor enim ex duobus cupiens dissolvi et esse cum Christo: multo enim hoc melius.
24. Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.
24. Manere vero in carne, magis necessarium propter vos.
25. And having this confidence, I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith;
25. Atque hoc confisus novi, quod manebo et permanebo cum omnibus vobis, in vestrum profectum et gaudium fidei,
26. That your rejoicing may be more abundant in Jesus Christ for me by my coming to you again.
26. Ut gloriatio vestra exsuperet in Christo Iesu de me, per meum rursus adventum ad vos.
entries.bcd5212dcf6af77d8a67b23056782d06cf69ea25: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.22" sID="gen126336" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22</hi> <hi type="italic">But if to live in the flesh</hi>. As persons in despair feel in perplexity as to whether they ought to prolong their life any farther in miseries, or to terminate their troubles by death, so Paul, on the other hand, says that he is, in a spirit of contentment, so well prepared for death or for life, because the condition of believers, both in the one case and in the other, is blessed, so that he is at a loss which to choose. <hi type="italic">If it is worth while;</hi> that is, “If I have reason to believe that there will be greater advantage from my life than from my death, I do not see which of them I ought to prefer.” <hi type="italic">To live in the flesh</hi>, is an expression which he has made use of in contempt, from comparing it with a better life.<div eID="gen126337" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126336" osisID="Phil.1.22" type="section"/>
entries.752556183a767cc35f052c4743310306ff538d09: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.23" sID="gen126338" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23</hi> <hi type="italic">For I am in a strait</hi> Paul did not desire to live with any other object in view that that of promoting the glory of Christ, and doing good to the brethren. Hence he does not reckon that he has any other advantage from living than the welfare of the brethren. But so far as concerns himself personally, it were, he acknowledges, better for him to die soon, because he would be <hi type="italic">with Christ.</hi> By his choice, however, he shews what ardent love glowed in his breast. There is nothing said here as to earthly advantages, but as to spiritual benefit, which is on good grounds supremely desirable in the view of the pious. Paul, however, as if forgetful of himself, does not merely hold himself undetermined, lest he should be swayed by a regard to his own benefit rather than that of the Philippians, but at length concludes that a regard to them preponderates in his mind. And assuredly this is in reality to live and die to Christ, when, with indifference as to ourselves, we allow ourselves to be carried and borne away withersoever Christ calls us.<div eID="gen126339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126340" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Having a desire to be set free and to be with Christ</hi> These two things must be read in connection. For death of itself will never be desired, because such a desire is at variance with natural feeling, but is desired for some particular reason, or with a view to some other end. Persons in despair have recourse to it from having become weary of life; believers, on the other hand, willingly hasten forward to it, because it is a deliverance from the bondage of sin, and an introduction into the kingdom of heaven. What Paul now says is this; “I desire to die, because I will, by this means, come into immediate connection with Christ.” In the mean time, believers do not cease to regard death with horror, but when they turn their eyes to that life which follows death, they easily overcome all dread by means of that consolation. Unquestionably, every one that believes in Christ ought to be so courageous as to <hi type="italic">lift up his head</hi> on mention being made of death, delighted to have intimation of his <hi type="italic">redemption</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.21.28">Luke 21:28</reference>.) From this we see how many are Christians only in name, since the greater part, on hearing mention made of death, are not merely alarmed, but are rendered almost lifeless through fear, as though they had never heard a single word respecting Christ. O the worth and value of a good conscience! Now faith is the foundation of a good conscience; nay more, it is itself goodness of conscience.<div eID="gen126340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126341" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To be set free</hi> This form of expression is to be observed. Profane persons speak of death as the destruction of man, as if he altogether perished. Paul here reminds us, that death is the separation of the soul from the body. And this he expresses more fully immediately afterwards, explaining as to what condition awaits believers after death — that of <hi type="italic">dwelling with Christ</hi> We are <hi type="italic">with Christ</hi> even in this life, inasmuch as the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God is within us</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.17.21">Luke 17:21</reference>,) and <hi type="italic">Christ dwells in us by faith,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.17">Ephesians 3:17</reference>,) and has promised that he <hi type="italic">will be with us even unto the end of the world</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.20">Matthew 28:20</reference>,) but that presence we enjoy only in hope. Hence as to our feeling, we are said to be at present at a <hi type="italic">distance</hi> from him. See <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.6">2 Corinthians 5:6</reference>. This passage is of use for setting aside the mad fancy of those who dream that souls sleep when separated from the body, for Paul openly declares that we enjoy Christ’s presence on being set free from the body.<div eID="gen126341" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126338" osisID="Phil.1.23" type="section"/>
entries.5eef209ce5a3a9f0c8fbd06dfd628cec7f6bafb7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.25" sID="gen126342" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25</hi> <hi type="italic">And having this confidence</hi>. Some, reckoning it an inconsistent thing that the Apostle <note n="82"> <div sID="gen126344" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn tel sainct Apostre</foreign>;” — “So holy an Apostle.”<div eID="gen126344" type="x-p"/> </note> should acknowledge himself to have been disappointed of his expectation, are of opinion that he was afterwards freed from bonds, and went over many countries of the world. Their fears, however, as to this are groundless, for the saints are accustomed to regulate their expectations according to the word of God, so as not to promise themselves more than God has promised. Thus, when they have a sure token of God’s will, they in that case place their reliance also upon a sure persuasion, which admits of no hesitation. Of this nature is a persuasion respecting a perpetual remission of sins, respecting the aid of the Spirit for the grace of final perseverance, (as it is called,) and respecting the resurrection of the flesh. Of this nature, also, was the assurance of the Prophets respecting their prophecies. As to other things, they expect nothing except conditionally, and hence they subject all events to the providence of God, who, they allow, sees more distinctly than they. To <hi type="italic">remain</hi>, means here, to stay for a little while: to <hi type="italic">continue</hi>, means, to remain for a long time.<div eID="gen126343" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126342" osisID="Phil.1.25" type="section"/>
entries.a2328d14dd472f14933a92e486059bb5471be3fe:
26 That your glorying. The expression which he employs, ἐν ἐμόι, I have rendered de me (as to me,) because the preposition is made use of twice, but in different senses. No one assuredly will deny that I have faithfully brought out Paul’s mind. The rendering given by some — per Christum, (through Christ,) I do not approve of. For in Christ is employed in place of Secundum Christum, (According to Christ,) or Christiane, (Christianly,) to intimate that it was a holy kind of glorying. For otherwise we are commanded to glory in God alone. (1 Corinthians 1:31.) Hence malevolent persons might meet Paul with the objection, How is it allowable for the Philippians to glory as to thee? He anticipates this calumny by saying that they will do this according to Christ — glorying in a servant of Christ, with a view to the glory of his Lord, and that with an eye to the doctrine rather than to the individual, and in opposition to the false apostles, just as David, by comparing himself with hypocrites, boasts of his righteousness. (Psalm 7:8.)
Philippians 1:27-30
27. Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
27. Tantum digne Evangelio Christi conversamini: ut sive veniens videam vos, sive absens, audiam de vobis, quod stetis in uno spiritu, una anima, concertantes fide Evangelii.
28. And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God.
28. Nec ulla in re terreamini ab adversariis, quae illis est demonstratio exitii: vobis autem salutis, idque a Deo.
29. For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;
29. Quia vobis donatum est pro Christo, non tantum ut in illum credatis, sed etiam ut pro ipso patiamini:
30. Having the same conflict which ye saw in me, and now hear to be in me.
30. Idem habentes certamen, quale vidistis in me, et nunc auditis de me.
entries.9378e0b9d4b79e6b1efe8d11b52e70ca48555106: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.27" sID="gen126358" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27</hi> <hi type="italic">Only in a manner worthy of the gospel</hi>. We make use of this form of expression, when we are inclined to pass on to a new subject. Thus it is as though he had said, “But as for me, the Lord will provide, but as for you, etc., whatever may take place as to me, let it be your care, nevertheless, to go forward in the right course.” When he speaks of a pure and honorable conversation as being worthy of the gospel, he intimates, on the other hand, that those who live otherwise do injustice to the gospel.<div eID="gen126359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126360" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That whether I come</hi> As the Greek phrase made use of by Paul is elliptical, I have made use of <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">videam</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, (I see,)</hi> instead of <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">videns</hi></foreign><hi type="italic"> (seeing.)</hi> If this does not appear satisfactory, you may supply the principal verb <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Intelligam</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, (I may learn,)</hi> in this sense: “Whether, when I shall come and see you, or whether I shall, when absent, hear respecting your condition, I may learn in both ways, both by being present and by receiving intelligence, that ye <hi type="italic">stand in one spirit.</hi>” We need not, however, feel anxiety as to particular terms, when the meaning is evident.<div eID="gen126360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126361" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Stand in one spirit</hi> This, certainly, is one of the main excellences of the Church, and hence this is one means of preserving it in a sound state, inasmuch as it is torn to pieces by dissensions. But although Paul was desirous by means of this antidote to provide against novel and strange doctrines, yet he requires a twofold unity — of <hi type="italic">spirit</hi> and <hi type="italic">soul</hi>. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> is, that we have like views; the <hi type="italic">second</hi>, that we be united in heart. For when these two terms are connected together, <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">spiritus</hi></foreign><hi type="italic"> (spirit)</hi> denotes the <hi type="italic">understanding</hi>, while <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">anima</hi></foreign><hi type="italic"> (soul)</hi> denotes the <hi type="italic">will</hi>. Farther, agreement of views comes first in order; and then from it springs union of inclination.<div eID="gen126361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126362" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Striving together for the faith</hi> This is the strongest bond of concord, when we have to fight together under the same banner, for this has often been the occasion of reconciling even the greatest enemies. Hence, in order that he may confirm the more the unity that existed among the Philippians, he calls them to notice that they are fellow-soldiers, who, having a common enemy and a common warfare, ought to have their minds united together in a holy agreement. The expression which Paul has made use of in the Greek (<foreign xml:lang="el">συναθλοῦντες τὣ πίστει</foreign>) is ambiguous. The old interpreter renders it <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Collaborantes fidei</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, (laboring together with the faith.)</hi> <note n="83"> <div sID="gen126363" type="x-p"/> In accordance with the Vulgate, Wiclif (1380) renders as follows: “traueilynge to gidre to the feith of the gospel.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen126363" type="x-p"/> </note> Erasmus renders it <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Adiuvantes fidem</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, (Helping the faith,)</hi> as if meaning, that they gave <hi type="italic">help</hi> to the <hi type="italic">faith</hi> to the utmost of their power. As, however, the dative in Greek is made use of instead of the ablative of instrumentality, (that language having no ablative,) I have no doubt that the Apostle’s meaning is this: “Let the faith of the gospel unite you together, more especially as that is a common armory against one and the same enemy.” In this way the particle <foreign xml:lang="el">σύν</foreign>, which others refer to <hi type="italic">faith</hi>, I take as referring to the Philippians, and with greater propriety, if I am not mistaken. In the first place, every one is aware how effectual an inducement it is to concord, when we have to maintain a conflict together; and farther, we know that in the spiritual warfare we are armed with the <hi type="italic">shield of faith</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.16">Ephesians 6:16</reference>,) for repelling the enemy; nay, more, faith is both our panoply and our victory. Hence he added this clause, that he might shew what is the end of a pious connection. The wicked, too, conspire together for evil, but their agreement is accursed: let us, therefore, contend with one mind under the banner of faith.<div eID="gen126362" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126358" osisID="Phil.1.27" type="section"/>
entries.3970984cf270b9f7fcdd2975d2261548b720c45f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.28" sID="gen126364" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28</hi> <hi type="italic">And in nothing terrified</hi>. The second thing which he recommends to the Philippians is fortitude of mind, <note n="84"> <div sID="gen126366" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La force et constance de courage</foreign>;” —”Strength and constancy of courage.”<div eID="gen126366" type="x-p"/> </note> that they may not be thrown into confusion by the rage of their adversaries. At that time the most cruel persecutions raged almost everywhere, because Satan strove with all his might to impede the commencement of the gospel, and was the more enraged in proportion as Christ put forth powerfully the grace of his Spirit. He exhorts, therefore, the Philippians to stand forward undaunted, and not be thrown into alarm.<div eID="gen126365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126367" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which is to them a manifest proof</hi>. This is the proper meaning of the Greek word, and there was no consideration that made it necessary for others to render it <hi type="italic">cause.</hi> For the wicked, when they wage war against the Lord, do already by a trial-fight, as it were, give a token of their ruin, and the more fiercely they insult over the pious, the more do they prepare themselves for ruin. The Scripture, assuredly, nowhere teaches, that the afflictions which the saints endure from the wicked are the <hi type="italic">cause</hi> of their salvation, but Paul in another instance, too, speaks of them as a <hi type="italic">manifest token</hi> or <hi type="italic">proof</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Thess.1.5">2 Thessalonians 1:5</reference>,) and instead of <foreign xml:lang="el">ἔνδειξιν</foreign>, which we have here, he in that passage makes use of the term <foreign xml:lang="el">ἔνδειγμα</foreign> <note n="85"> <div sID="gen126368" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Là où il vse d’vn mot qui descend d’vn mesme verbe que celuy dont il vse yci</foreign>;” —”Where he makes use of a word which comes from the same verb as that which he employs here.”<div eID="gen126368" type="x-p"/> </note> This, therefore, is a choice consolation, that when we are assailed and harassed by our enemies, we have an evidence of our salvation. <note n="86"> <div sID="gen126369" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Cela nous est vne demonstrance et tesmoignage de nostre salut</foreign>;” —”This is to us a clear proof and token of our salvation.”<div eID="gen126369" type="x-p"/> </note> For persecutions are in a manner seals of adoption to the children of God, if they endure them with fortitude and patience: the wicked give a token of their condemnation, because they stumble against a stone by which they shall be bruised to pieces. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.44">Matthew 21:44</reference>.)<div eID="gen126367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126370" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And that from God</hi>. This is restricted to the last clause, that a taste of the grace of God may allay the bitterness of the cross. No one will naturally perceive the cross a token or evidence of salvation, for they are things that are contrary in appearance. Hence Paul calls the attention of the Philippians to another consideration — that God by his blessing turns into an occasion of welfare things that might otherwise seem to render us miserable. He proves it from this, that the endurance of the cross is the gift of God. Now it is certain, that all the gifts of God are salutary to us. <hi type="italic">To you</hi>, says he,<hi type="italic"> it is given, not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him.</hi> Hence even the sufferings themselves are evidences of the grace of God; and, since it is so, you have from this source a token of salvation. Oh, if this persuasion were effectually inwrought in our minds — that persecutions <note n="87"> <div sID="gen126371" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les afflictions et persecutions</foreign>;” — “Afflictions and persecutions.”<div eID="gen126371" type="x-p"/> </note> are to be reckoned among God’s benefits, what progress would be made in the doctrine of piety! <note n="88"> <div sID="gen126372" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Combien aurions — nous proufité en la doctrine de vraye religion</foreign>;” —”How much progress we would make in the doctrine of true religion.”<div eID="gen126372" type="x-p"/> </note> And yet, what is more certain, than that it is the highest honor that is conferred upon us by Divine grace, that we suffer for his name either reproach, or imprisonment, or miseries, or tortures, or even death, for in that case he adorns us with his marks of distinction. <note n="89"> <div sID="gen126373" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il nous vest de sa liuree</foreign>;” — “He arrays us in his livery.”<div eID="gen126373" type="x-p"/> </note> But more will be found that will rather bid God retire with gifts of that nature, than embrace with alacrity the cross when it is presented to them. Alas, then, for our stupidity! <note n="90"> <div sID="gen126374" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Maudite donc soit nostre stupidite</foreign>;” — “Accursed, then, be our stupidity.”<div eID="gen126374" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen126370" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126364" osisID="Phil.1.28" type="section"/>
entries.526446c40c4028a3579ba25213ce5c8c66008486: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.1.29" sID="gen126375" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29. </hi><hi type="italic">To believe</hi>. He wisely conjoins faith with the cross by an inseparable connection, that the Philippians may know that they have been called to the faith of Christ on this condition — that they endure persecutions on his account, as though he had said that their adoption can no more be separated from the cross, than Christ can be torn asunder from himself. Here Paul clearly testifies, that faith, as well as constancy in enduring persecutions, <note n="91"> <div sID="gen126377" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les afflictions et persecutions</foreign>;” — “Afflictions and persecutions.”<div eID="gen126377" type="x-p"/> </note> is an unmerited gift of God. And certainly the knowledge of God is a wisdom that is too high for our attaining it by our own acuteness, and our weakness shews itself in daily instances in our own experience, when God withdraws his hand for a little while. That he may intimate the more distinctly that both are unmerited, he says expressly — for Christ’s sake, or at least that they are given to us on the ground of Christ’s grace; by which he excludes every idea of merit.<div eID="gen126376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126378" type="x-p"/>This passage is also at variance with the doctrine of the schoolmen, in maintaining that gifts of grace latterly conferred are rewards of our merit, on the ground of our having made a right use of those which had been previously bestowed. I do not deny, indeed, that God rewards the right use of his gifts of grace by bestowing grace more largely upon us, provided only you do not place merit, as they do, in opposition to his unmerited liberality and the merit of Christ.<div eID="gen126378" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.1.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126375" osisID="Phil.1.29" type="section"/>

30 Having the same conflict. He confirms, also, by his own example what he had said, and this adds no little authority to his doctrine. By the same means, too, he shews them, that there is no reason why they should feel troubled on account of his bonds, when they behold the issue of the conflict.
CHAPTER 2
Philippians 2:1-4
1. If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels and mercies,
1. Si qua igitur consolatio (vel, exhortatio) in Christo, si quod solatium dilectionis, si qua communicatio Spiritus, si qua viscera et misericordiae.
“Entrailles et misericordes, ou, cordiales affections et misericordes;” — “Bowels and mercies, or, cordial affections and mercies.”
2. Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind.
2. Implete gaudium meum ut idem sentiatis, eandem habentes caritatem, unanimes, unum sentientes.
3 Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
3. Nihil per contentionem, aut inanem gloriam, sed per humilitatem alii alios existiment se ipsis excellentiores.
4. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
4. Non considerans quisque quod suum est, sed quisque quod est aliorum.

               <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">PAUL and Timotheus <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.1. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.1. The Authour and approver intimating the good agreement 'twixt <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> whom they well knew, to gain their fuller assent to what should be written, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.16.</ns0:note> the servants of Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In a special manner being wholly and perpetually dedicated to his more immedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ate service in the Ministry of Reconciliation, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 13.2. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.1. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.1. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.18. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.1. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.1.</ns0:note>, to all the saints in Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All the Community of Church members at <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> called out of the World to Christ, sanctified, separated and dedicated to him, by a credible profession of faith in him and obedience to him, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.2. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.1. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.2. The Apos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle now being well perswaded of their perseverance, <ns0:hi>Vers.</ns0:hi> 6, 7.</ns0:note>, which are at Philippi, with the bishops, and deacons <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">From the <ns0:hi>Syriac</ns0:hi> version it is rendred Pres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />byters and Ministers. And there appears no cogent rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son why we should not adhere to the exposition of Ancient and Modern Interpreters, who understand the Apostle wri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting in the Plural Number particularly to the Church and her Officers living in this City, as meaning the <ns0:hi>two</ns0:hi> Orders of ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary standing Officers, which are appointed for the Church, and not the Church for the Officers. By the former of which are meant such Pastours and Teachers as did agree in Name, Office, and Power with the Bishops during the Apostles times, as they collect from several other Scriptures besides this compar'd together, <ns0:hi>viz<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Act.</ns0:hi> 20.17, 20, 25, 28. with 11.30. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.1. and 12.28. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.12, 13. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.1. to 8. and 5.17. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.5, 7. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.17. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 5.14. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.2, 3. 3 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.9. These whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Bishops or Elders having the Oversight, Rule, Gui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dance, Feeding of the People, Preaching of the Word, and Administration of the Sacraments or Mystical ordinances of the Gospel committed to them in common. By the latter, those to whom the special care was committed for serving of Tables, the Lord's Table and the Poors, together with a re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiving and orderly disposing and distributing the collected Alms and other goods of theChurch given to pious uses accor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding to their own discretion, taking advice of the Pastours for the support and benefit of the poor Members of the Church who needed as to this temporal life, to orphans, widows, yea and strangers, especially of the houshold of Faith, that their bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dily necessities might be supplyed, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 6.4. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.7, 8. & 15, 25, 26, 27. & 16.1. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.28. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.1, 2.12. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.8. with 1. <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.10, 11. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 2.1, 25, 30. with 4.18. <ns0:hi>Iude.</ns0:hi> 12.
<ns0:q> But <ns0:hi>two</ns0:hi> learned Doctours amongst us have oppos'd this and made it difficult, the <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> by restraining the word Bi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shops to Diocesans, and the <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> by enlarging the word Deacons to note their Presbyters. He would have no such order of Presbyters, as now, in the Apostles days; <ns0:hi>This</ns0:hi> would have Deacons <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> to be onely temporary not stan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding Officers in the Church, and so they agree not. The former finding <ns0:hi>Clement</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Polycarp</ns0:hi> agreed with the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle here, as to <ns0:hi>two</ns0:hi> distinct orders of Bishops and Deacons, going upon an unprov'd Supposition that <ns0:hi>Philippi</ns0:hi> was then a <ns0:hi>Metropolis,</ns0:hi> he would, without any satisfactory evidence to one that doubted, infer the Bishops here were Diocesans, however the fore-mentioned scriptures compar'd, all prove the words Bishop and Elder in the Apostles days, to be used promiscuously, onely the word Elders, or Presbyters, more frequently than that of Bishops, concieving that the Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice of Presbyters was not in use till after ages, though he assigns not the time how and when it came in. So that in effect he would have <ns0:hi>Philippi</ns0:hi> to be a mother Church, (that then had several daughter Churches) in her infancy. Whereas the Apostle writes to those who were Church-officers in that City; yet he would have them none of that Order which we now call Presbyters; thinking whatever the Apostle writes of laying on the hands of the Presbytery, there were then no Presbyters ordained in the Church: which is a singular opinion of holding all the places in the N. T. where Presbyters are named, precisely to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend Diocesan Bishops in distinction from them who are onely Deacons, allowing the Office of Deacons, and the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinuance of it to be appointed therein, when that of Elders (acknowledged to be Superiour) is not. But if according to this Novel tenet there were not <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> Preaching Presbyters, that were not <ns0:hi>Metropolitans</ns0:hi> or Diocesans, how could Dio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cesans have Presbyters under them? and if they had none what should denominate them properly Diocesans? when it seems to be of the formal reason of a Diocesan to be cho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sen out of Presbyters or to have them to Govern. And if the Diocesan Bishops where then as the Apostles, who must the Pastours and Teachers be? 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.28, 29. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.11, 12. Exhorting, Teaching, Ruling were then present Offices which the Apostles ordained in every Church, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 14.23. <ns0:hi>Cenchrea</ns0:hi> was no Diocese or Metropolis, neither was <ns0:hi>Aquila</ns0:hi>'s and <ns0:hi>Priscilla</ns0:hi>'s house, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.3, 4. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.19. yet are said to be Churches in the plural number, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.33, 34. If Metropo litical or Diocesan, how hath not the Scripture the name or thing? This appears not to be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />greeable to the Apostles way, who writes particularly to Churches in Cities, Towns, and Countries, as to the <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brews.</ns0:hi> He distinguisheth <ns0:hi>Thessalonica,</ns0:hi> in directions from <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Achaia,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.7, 8. <ns0:hi>Colosse</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Laodi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cea, Col.</ns0:hi> 4..13. And as there were Bishops plural in this Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty of <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> so more doeing the Office in <ns0:hi>Thessalonica,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.12. which was in <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> too. And would it not look odly, ye Christians of <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> are examples to all the Christians of <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> In <ns0:hi>Coloss.</ns0:hi> were more Bi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shops or Presbyters because there is mention made of <ns0:hi>Epa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phras</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Archippus? Col.</ns0:hi> 4.12, 17. And would it not appear strange, when they were charg'd upon Persons be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Sick, to send for the Elders of the Church, to conclude the intent of the injunction was to send for all the Dioce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sans of the Metropolis? <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 5.14. If so, he would like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly have enjoyn'd them to have call'd the Elders of the Churches, not of the Church, of which in the Singular at <ns0:hi>Hierusalem Paul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Barnabas</ns0:hi> were received, and of the Apostles and Elders, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 15.4. who were all present at <ns0:hi>Hierusalem, Act.</ns0:hi> 21.18. which under the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> power, was not the Metropolis of <ns0:hi>Palestine,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Caesarea</ns0:hi> was chief. The <ns0:hi>latter</ns0:hi> contradictory to the former Doctor, and to the <ns0:hi>Office</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Church of England</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>ordaining of Dea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cons,</ns0:hi> would have the term <ns0:hi>Deacons</ns0:hi> to note the <ns0:hi>order of Presbyters,</ns0:hi> looking upon Deacons onely as temporary and occasional trustees, whose Office <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> in his Epistle did not so much as hint, thinking it unreasonable by Deacon in those Epistles to understand any other Office than that of Presbyters as now used. Whereas the word <ns0:hi>Deacons</ns0:hi> being Analogous and put absolutely here, in contradistinction to Bishops, should according: to right reason be expounded in the most famous and distinctive Signification, wherein, no doubt <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> a good <ns0:hi>Graecian,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s Companion at <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lippi,</ns0:hi> used it in the <ns0:hi>Acts,</ns0:hi> 6.3, 4, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Written after this Epis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle, unto which special import we should rather understand <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> using it here, for those who were not mere occasional and prudential temporary Officers, but such as were to abide in the Church. Wherein upon the multiplying of De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sciples, the bodily necessities of the Saints always with us <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.8. did require such who should have the peculiar care of these committed to them, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20.34, 35. We find the Apostle in his Epistles evidently enough appointing and describing such a special Ministry, yea and giving directions about it as a distinct branch from prophecy, and teaching, if we compare places, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.6, 7, 8. with 15.26, 27. &. 16.1. & 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.19. &. 9.1, 2, 12. and what is said in this Epistle, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 2.25, 30. & 4.18. answerable to <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi>'s history of <ns0:hi>the Acts,</ns0:hi> and to what is written by <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.11. taking in what <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> wrote to Timothy about this Officer in distinction from his who was to be apt to teach, that he should be Grave, Tempe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rate, giving proof of Freedom from Covetousness, of Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation blameless, having a faithfull Wife, and gover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning his Family (that he may be Hospital) orderly, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.8. to 13. qualified to distribute, as in the Texts fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mentioned, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> The Church of <ns0:hi>England</ns0:hi> in her <ns0:hi>Ordination</ns0:hi> hath reference to this special Office, when yet it calls Deacons, Ministers, declaring <ns0:hi>there, It appertains to the Deacons Office to assist the Presbyter in distribution of the Elements, gladly and willingly to search for the Poor, Sick and Impotent, that they may be reliev'd. Praying that they may be modest, humble and constant in their mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistration.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:q>

               <ns0:p n="4">4 (Always in every prayer of mine for you all making request with joy <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As in praising of God, the Authour of all that Grace they had received, in every solemn Prayer, so in continuing his fervent and assiduous requests unto God, wait, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.17. for them all.                <ns0:p n="5">5 For your fellowship in the gospel, from the first day until now <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Your being joined with us and other Christians in the Communion of Christ, and glad tidings of Salvation by him, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.16, 17. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.3, 7. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.13. evidenc'd by the Communication of your bounty, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.6. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.16. much as both <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">2 Tim. 1.8.</ns0:note> in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">O<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
